newsitem.title: USA: Denver's Muse urges Congress to look at muni laws.
newsitem.headline: Denver's Muse urges Congress to look at muni laws.

text.p: Denver's top attorney said it is time for the U.S. Congress to make clear whether it intended to give the SEC authority to bring securities fraud charges against municipalities.

Denver City Attorney Daniel Muse, fresh from a victory in the Securities and Exchange Commission's two-year-old probe of Denver International Airport, made the recommendation during a speech before the International Municipal Lawyers Association here on Monday.

SEC staff on October 4 notified Denver officials that it has dropped its investigation of whether the city violated securities fraud laws by not disclosing to bond investors potential problems with a troubled, hi-tech baggage system.

Muse said rather than continue to spend "vast sums of money" on municipal bond probes, SEC should ask Congress to clarify whether securities fraud laws apply to state and local governments issuing bonds.

The lack of clarity has caused a "furor" over SEC jurisdiction in the area, said Muse. He said he does not think SEC has authority over localities, but "there is room for disagreement" over the issue because of "ambiguity" on Capitol Hill.

If SEC has authority over municipalities, why has it not brought cases against general purpose issuers before now, Muse asked. "The problems the Commission suddenly has raised about the adequacy of disclosure didn't magically appear in 1994," Muse said.
He said Denver's disclosure has "dramatically improved" since since 1975 when Congress enacted the so-called Tower Amendment to the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.
That amendment bars SEC, in effect, from regulating municipal bond issuers.

"(SEC's) failure to undertake enforcement actions for nearly 20 years, particularly in light of the catastrophic losses incurred in the New York City and Washington Public Power Supply System cases make you wonder whether the Commission is sure they actually have jurisdiction," Muse said.
"This failure to assert jurisdiction has contributed substantially to the furor about SEC jurisdiction," Muse added.
